The name occurs 14 times in the Hebrew corpus, across seven verses, including references in Joshua, 1 Samuel, and Hosea. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its ordinary function is to designate this location by name.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “parts,” identifying portions treated separately rather than as one whole. It is an Old Testament word found three times, in Genesis and Jeremiah. Its uses are connected with parts being given in significant actions, so the word points to divided portions that have a role in what is being done. The precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to Bat-shua, a personal name appearing in a biblical genealogy. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, both within 1 Chronicles 3:5. In that passage, the name is connected with a birth or begetting relationship and therefore identifies a person within a family record. The available lexical information does not provide a separate gloss or short definition for the name, so its ordinary meaning as a personal name cannot be stated more precisely here. Its scriptural use is chiefly genealogical identification.

e.t: This word refers to Galilee, the name of a region in the Old Testament. It functions as a place-name rather than describing an action or quality. The word appears six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in passages naming or referring to Galilee in Joshua, Kings, Chronicles, and Isaiah. Its use includes references to the region as a place connected with Israel’s tribal lands and with events involving its rulers and inhabitants.

This Hebrew word means “also.” It functions as an adding word, connecting one statement or circumstance with another and indicating that the added point belongs alongside what has already been said. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Psalm 119:20 and Lamentations 3:16. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic role is to add or include another point rather than introduce a separate subject.

The word refers to “Dura,” a proper name rather than a general description or action. It functions as the name of a place identified in the Hebrew Old Testament. This word occurs only once in the Hebrew corpus, in Daniel 3:1, so Scripture provides no wider range of uses for it. Its meaning is therefore limited and straightforward: “Dura,” the named location mentioned in that passage.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “tears,” referring to the drops shed from the eyes. It names tears as a recognizable expression of human sorrow, distress, or grief, though the surrounding passage determines the particular reason for them. The word occurs 23 times in the Hebrew Bible, appearing especially in Psalms, Jeremiah, Isaiah, and Lamentations. Its repeated use in prayers and descriptions of suffering shows how tears are presented openly before God rather than hidden from him.

Hadassah is a personal name, rendered “Hadassah.” In the Hebrew Bible, this word appears once, at Esther 2:7, so its ordinary use is as a specific name rather than a frequently repeated description or action. The available wording does not establish an additional English meaning beyond the name itself. Its significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, while the word’s lexical role is simply to identify Hadassah.

Vashni is a Hebrew personal name, functioning as the identifying name of an individual rather than as a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 6:28. “Vashni” is the only supported rendering, and no explicit definition is given for the name. The word’s recorded use does not establish an additional ordinary meaning beyond identifying this person.

This Hebrew word means “proud.” It is a descriptive word used to characterize something as proud rather than naming a person, place, or action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 124:5. The rendering “proud” appears consistently for this occurrence, supporting that central meaning. Its precise force in Psalm 124:5 depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “herbs,” functioning as a noun that names plants gathered or present in a setting. It occurs four times in the Old Testament, appearing once each in 2 Kings, Esther, Psalms, and Isaiah. Its clearest repeated rendering is “herbs,” and its precise role in any individual verse depends on the surrounding context. The word therefore points to herbs as a concrete thing rather than expressing an action, quality, or person.

This Hebrew word means “new.” It functions as a descriptive word, identifying something as new rather than naming an object or action. In the Hebrew Old Testament represented here, it occurs once, in Ezra 6:4. The available English rendering is consistently “new,” making that the clearest ordinary sense. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself contributes the idea of newness to whatever noun it describes.

This Hebrew word means “kernels,” naming the individual parts of something rather than an action, quality, or person. It is a concrete noun used once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Numbers 6:4. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s exact contextual force cannot be described further. Its basic sense remains a specific tangible item identified as kernels, and the reference confirms that this is its sole recorded Old Testament occurrence.

The word refers to “Talmon,” a Hebrew proper name rather than an ordinary descriptive term. It identifies a named individual or family designation in Old Testament records. The name occurs five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in 1 Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah. Since no separate definition or descriptive gloss is given, its supported meaning is simply the personal name “Talmon,” and its precise reference depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word is a personal name, referring to Jehoiachin, the king named in the Old Testament. It occurs ten times, entirely within the Old Testament, especially in 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles, and Jeremiah. The name is consistently rendered “Jehoiachin,” so it identifies a particular historical person rather than expressing a general idea or action. Its occurrences begin in 2 Kings 24:6 and continue through Jeremiah 52:31, with related passages describing him as someone who reigned and was later released from imprisonment. The surrounding verse determines the specific detail being stated about him.

e.t: Jehoshaphat is a personal name, rendered consistently as “Jehoshaphat.” It identifies people in the Hebrew Old Testament rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs 84 times across 75 verses, especially in the historical books. Its appearances include references to a king of Judah and other individuals who bear the same name; the surrounding passage identifies which person is intended. The word’s basic function is therefore to name a person.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “day.” It functions as a noun for identifying a day within the biblical account, whether marking a calendar setting, a period of events, or a stated occasion. It is very common in the Hebrew Old Testament, occurring 2,302 times, so its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding words and context. Its broad use includes statements, commands, and descriptions of events.

This Hebrew verb describes an action associated with a person’s inner self and appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Jeremiah 4:31. Its precise English meaning cannot be stated confidently from the available lexical information alone. In that occurrence, it is connected with the soul and with expressions involving a voice and a hand, showing that it describes an action or expression rather than a person or object. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain its exact force there.

This Hebrew word means “shut.” It describes closing or blocking something so that passage or access is stopped. In its only Old Testament occurrence, it functions as an action word in Psalm 69:15. The surrounding verse determines precisely what is being shut, but the word itself centers on the act of closing or preventing an opening. Its use is limited to that single occurrence in the Hebrew Old Testament.

e.t: This word means “month”. It is a noun naming a period of time used to mark dates, the passing of seasons, or the timing of events. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 13 times and is ordinarily rendered “month.” Its use includes references to a person’s age, appointed times, and the progress of building or worship. The word may also be associated with the moon’s cycle, which helps explain its connection with calendar time. [p03:word:hebrew:H3391:renderings] [p03:word:hebrew:H3391:occurrences]

e.t: This Hebrew word is a personal name rather than a general action, quality, or object. It refers to a named individual in the Old Testament and appears three times within 2 Samuel 21:16. The available material identifies it with the phrase יִשְׁבּוֹ בְּנֹב, but does not provide an English definition or enough surrounding verse text to explain the name’s literal components. Its precise role in that passage depends on the full context.

This Hebrew word expresses “casting,” functioning as an action word for something being done. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Micah 6:14. Because the available lexical information is limited and the verse text is not included here, its exact force in that sentence must be understood from the surrounding context. Its central meaning is the action of casting, not a person, place, or quality.

This Hebrew word means “cut,” expressing the action of cutting. It occurs only twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, once in Psalm 80:16 and once in Isaiah 33:12. In both places, its recognized English rendering is “cut,” giving it a direct and concrete sense rather than a broad or abstract one. The precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains the act of cutting. It is best understood as an action word describing cutting.

This Hebrew word functions as “would,” marking a statement about what is desired, imagined, or conditional rather than simply stating a present fact. It appears 25 times in the Old Testament, across 22 verses, so it serves as a recurring way to frame wishes or possible situations. Its exact force depends on the sentence in which it occurs, but its central contribution is to present an outcome as contemplated rather than directly asserted.

This Hebrew word means “kindred.” It identifies people connected to someone through family relationship and functions as a noun referring to that relationship or group of people. The word appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ruth 3:2, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated occurrences. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea is family connection.

This Hebrew word refers to “foundations,” the supporting base on which something rests or is established. It functions as a term for a firm underlying support rather than an action or quality. The word occurs twice in the Old Testament, once in Isaiah 30:32 and once in Ezekiel 41:8. Its use in these passages points to something grounded, stable, and structurally supporting. The precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

It names the thing that can trip someone up or lead them into difficulty. The word occurs 14 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages in Leviticus, Psalms, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel. Its exact force in any verse is clarified by the surrounding sentence and passage.

The word occurs 28 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages about offerings, boundaries, land, and speech. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary lexical meaning remains salt.

Scripture uses it in passages concerning the body, death, and what is located within a person. It also appears in language describing something being placed within the bowels, showing that the word can identify the inner bodily region rather than an outward part.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “little,” expressing a small amount, size, or degree. It can describe something limited in quantity or extent, and it may function in statements about people, possessions, time, or circumstances. The word occurs 101 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing regular use for what is small or not abundant. Its exact force in a sentence depends on the surrounding words and context.

This Hebrew word expresses “going,” describing movement or departure rather than naming a person or object. It functions as an action word in its one occurrence in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Daniel 6:14. Because a fuller lexical definition and the verse text are not available here, the safest understanding is its basic verbal idea: going. Its precise force in Daniel 6:14 depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Elienai is a personal name, used to identify an individual rather than describe an action, object, or quality. In the Hebrew Bible, this name appears once, in 1 Chronicles 8:20, and is rendered “Elienai.” The available wording does not provide a separate ordinary-word definition or explain the name’s underlying sense. Its role is therefore primarily identifying: it distinguishes this person from others named in the surrounding record. The passage context would be needed to say more about the individual or the name’s significance.

This Hebrew word refers to “anguish,” describing a condition of intense distress. It names the painful state itself, rather than identifying a person, place, or action. The word occurs seven times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing that it expresses a recognizable human experience across several passages. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording and situation.

Maralah is a Hebrew proper name rendered “Maralah,” rather than an ordinary descriptive word translated into English. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Joshua 19:11. Because it appears as a named term, its meaning for readers is chiefly its identification of Maralah itself; the surrounding verse would be needed to explain its specific role there. This word is therefore best understood as a distinct biblical name, not as a general action, quality, or object.

This Hebrew word means “forsaken.” It describes someone or something as left in that condition, functioning as a descriptive term rather than naming an action. Its precise force in a particular sentence depends on the surrounding context. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 51:5, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated passages within this corpus.

This Hebrew verb means “lead.” It describes an action in which someone causes or directs people, animals, or other things to go from one place or situation to another. The word is used 31 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its basic sense applies across several kinds of movement and guidance. Its precise force in any verse depends on what is being led and where it is going.

e.t: This Hebrew word is the personal name “Noah.” It identifies the man who appears prominently in Genesis and is also mentioned later in Isaiah, 1 Chronicles, and Ezekiel. The name is used for Noah himself and in possessive form for something belonging to him. Within the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 46 times, mostly in Genesis. Its uses are connected with Noah’s family, God’s commands involving him, and the account of his death.

Its precise sense therefore depends on the verse’s wording and surrounding context.

e.t: This Hebrew word is the personal name “Absalom,” referring to a man rather than describing an action or quality. It functions as a proper name throughout the Old Testament, most often in the account of David’s son. The name appears 110 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with most occurrences in 2 Samuel. Its surrounding passages connect it with family relationships, royal speech, commands, and conflict, but those details belong to the individual contexts rather than changing the word’s basic meaning as a personal name.

This Hebrew word means “flowers.” It is a noun naming flowers, and its only recorded Hebrew Old Testament occurrence is in Song of Songs 2:12. The word therefore has a narrow attested use in this corpus, while its basic meaning is straightforward. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context, which are not included here.

This word expresses a limited idea whose exact sense depends on its context. Its precise English meaning cannot be stated confidently from the available lexical information alone. It appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Song of Solomon 7:3, so its normal usage cannot be compared across multiple passages. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine how the word functions there. It should therefore be understood cautiously, without assigning it an unsupported synonym or broader theological meaning.

This word expresses something being consumed or fulfilled—brought to its completed end. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Daniel. English renderings present it as “consume” in Daniel 2:44 and “fulfilled” in Daniel 4:33, showing that its precise sense depends on what is being brought to an end: something may be consumed, or a stated matter may reach completion. Its basic idea is completion through an ending.

This Hebrew word describes something as “endangered” or “impoverished.” It points to a condition in which a person or thing is exposed to loss, danger, or lack. In the Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Ecclesiastes and once in Isaiah. Its use can describe something at risk or something reduced to poverty, depending on the sentence in which it appears. The surrounding verse determines which aspect is most prominent.

This Hebrew word marks the point or limit up to which something extends, happens, or continues. It functions as a relational word, connecting an action, place, or time with its endpoint. Its dominant rendering is “unto.” It is common in the Hebrew Old Testament, occurring 1,263 times, so it serves this boundary-marking role across many kinds of statements rather than describing a person, object, or action by itself.

This Hebrew word means “they,” functioning as a pronoun for more than one person. It refers to a group rather than a single individual and can stand in for that group in a sentence. The word occurs four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing once in Ezra and three times in Daniel. Its precise reference in any passage depends on the surrounding sentence and context.

Ezri is a Hebrew personal name, referring to one individual rather than describing a general idea, action, or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 27:26, and the English renderings preserve it as “Ezri.” Because no explicit lexical definition is available here, the name itself is the supported meaning; its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word means “fainted.” It describes a person becoming physically overcome and losing strength. In the Old Testament, it occurs five times, serving as a verb that expresses this condition rather than naming a person or object. Its uses range across Genesis, Song of Solomon, Isaiah, Amos, and Jonah, so the word can describe weakness in different situations while retaining the central idea of becoming faint.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “pillars,” referring to upright structural elements. It is a noun used for individual supports as well as groups of supports, especially in descriptions of the tabernacle, temple, and other buildings. The word occurs 112 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a consistent reference to pillars as physical parts of constructed spaces. Its surrounding context determines the particular building or arrangement intended.

“Amramites” is a plural noun naming a group of people identified with Amram. It functions as a family or lineage designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Numbers and 1 Chronicles, and is rendered “Amramites” in each recorded translation alignment. The word therefore points to people belonging to the Amramite group, while the surrounding verse supplies the specific setting in which they are mentioned.

“Ananiah” is a personal name used in the Hebrew Old Testament. It appears twice, both times in Nehemiah, at Nehemiah 3:23 and 11:32. The available wording preserves it as “Ananiah,” so its ordinary role is to identify a person, not to describe an action, quality, or object. Because no explicit definition is given, the safest explanation is that this word functions as a personal name.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “heaps,” referring to quantities gathered together. It functions as a noun, naming something collected rather than an action. It occurs eleven times in the Old Testament and is consistently rendered “heaps.” Several occurrences are connected with giving and gathered offerings, while others refer to a heap in a different setting. Its ordinary sense is therefore a visible accumulation, with the surrounding verse showing what has been gathered.

e.t: This Hebrew word is the personal name “Athaliah,” referring to a woman in the Old Testament rather than expressing a general idea or action. It functions as a proper name and appears 17 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, across Kings, Chronicles, and Ezra. Its occurrences are connected with the historical figure Athaliah and with references to her in accounts involving royal succession, death, and the preservation of a child. The name itself should therefore be understood as identifying a person; its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “opened,” describing an opening action or condition. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs four times, including passages in Job, Psalms, and Isaiah. Its use can refer to something being opened broadly rather than merely making a small gap, but the exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording. It functions as a Hebrew word for expressing opening.

This Hebrew word refers to villages—settled communities or small population centers. It functions as a place-related noun rather than describing a person, action, or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Habakkuk 3:14, so its meaning is narrowly attested. The surrounding verse would determine the precise force of the reference, but the word itself identifies villages as the places being mentioned.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to the foot, the part of the body used for standing and walking. It can also identify the lower extremity more specifically, as when referring to a toe. The word occurs 251 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so it is a common bodily term rather than a rare or specialized expression. Its wider scriptural use includes physical movement, standing, falling, and the placement or condition of a person’s feet, with the precise sense determined by the surrounding sentence.

This Hebrew noun refers to a “gutter” or “trough,” a physical structure associated with water. It appears four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Genesis, Exodus, and Song of Songs. Its uses point to an ordinary object rather than an action or abstract idea. The exact nuance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central meaning is a water-channel or trough.

This Hebrew verb expresses making something “large.” It functions as an action word, describing an increase in size or extent, whether used of physical space or another subject whose scope is enlarged. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 25 times across 25 verses, so its basic idea appears in several settings rather than belonging to one narrow passage. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and context.

This Hebrew word expresses the idea of “lengthening,” referring to making something longer or allowing it to continue for a greater period. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Daniel. As a word with this meaning, its precise sense in either verse depends on what is being lengthened and the surrounding sentence. The available occurrences are Daniel 4:27 and Daniel 7:12, but the verse text is needed to explain the specific force in each passage.

Resheph is a Hebrew name rendered as “Resheph,” rather than as an ordinary descriptive word. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at 1 Chronicles 7:25. The available lexical record gives no broader definition, so its clearest meaning is the identification of Resheph as a name. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context, which is not included here.

“Shuni” is a personal name, identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, and English renderings preserve it as “Shuni.” The name itself is presented without an explicit definition, so it should be understood as a proper name rather than a translatable description. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding family and genealogical context.

This Hebrew word means “bribe.” It functions as a noun describing something offered to influence another person’s action or decision. In its two Old Testament occurrences, it appears once in Job and once in Ezekiel, showing this ordinary sense across both uses. The word is associated with conduct intended to gain favor or obtain a desired response through what is offered, rather than through a rightful decision. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

The Hebrew word means “forget.” It expresses forgetting as a biblical action, while the surrounding passage determines what is being forgotten and how strongly the word applies. It occurs twice in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, in Psalm 9:17 and Isaiah 65:11. Those references establish its limited range, but without the verse text they do not add further meaning beyond the basic word sense.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “tooth,” referring to one of the hard structures in the mouth. It is used 55 times in the Hebrew Old Testament and can also appear in descriptions of teeth, biting, or tooth-like features. In some passages, the word is connected with physical harm or loss, while elsewhere it is associated with crafted objects or prominent rocky forms. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

e.t: The Hebrew word means “for” and functions as a word that connects an expression with its intended relation. In the Old Testament, it occurs 48 times, so its exact force is determined by the sentence in which it appears. It is found in passages involving commands, giving, speech, and relationships, but the surrounding verse is needed to identify its particular use.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “Blessed.” It is used to declare a person or people to be in a blessed condition, often in statements that recognize the goodness of their situation before God. It functions as a descriptive word or blessing declaration rather than naming an action or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 45 times, especially in Psalms and Proverbs, where it commonly identifies those whose position or way is presented as truly blessed.

This Hebrew word means to “mark” or “point,” referring to identifying a particular location or boundary point. It is a rare Old Testament word, occurring only twice, both times in Numbers 34:7–8. In those uses, it functions as an expression for specifying a place rather than describing a person, object, or general action. Its basic sense is therefore a designated point or the act of marking one. The surrounding verse text would clarify its exact role in each sentence.

Asareel is a personal name preserved in the Hebrew Old Testament, rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies one individual in the genealogy recorded at 1 Chronicles 4:16. The available wording does not provide a broader lexical definition or explain the name’s etymology, so its safest ordinary meaning is simply the person’s name, rendered “Asareel.” It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament.

It occurs 32 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, across 30 verses. Its uses include sacrificial and communal settings, so the word points to a presented offering rather than an action or description.

In the Old Testament, it appears 34 times, showing a broad use for hope in different situations rather than a term limited to one setting. Scripture presents hope as something that may be expressed in speech and associated with what is given by God, while its precise force in a verse depends on the surrounding context.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a governor, a governing official. “Tirshatha” is another rendering of the same title, rather than a separate kind of person. In its five Old Testament occurrences, it identifies an official connected with the community’s leadership, including situations involving speech, giving, and formal commitment. The word appears in Ezra and Nehemiah, where it functions as a title for the person holding authority. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.
